item.title: Cognitive Selfhood: The Last Human Right
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Cognitive Selfhood: The Last Human Right

As AI takes on more thinking, what happens to the self doing the thinking?

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • AI is changing how we think and how we experience ourselves.
  • Cognitive selfhood means remaining meaningfully present in our own thinking.
  • Every human right begins with a self that is there to hold it.
Source: Leroy Skalstad / Pixabay

Over 100 years ago, Auguste Deter sat across from the physician Alois Alzheimer, struggling to answer simple questions about her life. Her memory was failing, along with other elements of cognition that most of us take for granted. At one point, she offered a remarkable description of what was happening to her: “I have, so to speak, lost myself.”

Her words are powerful and resonant. She didn’t simply say that she had lost her memory or couldn’t remember. She said she had lost herself. Alzheimer’s disease is much more complicated than memory loss, but her words point toward something we almost intuitively understand. Cognition isn’t simply something the self possesses; it’s part of how the self is constructed and experienced.

We tend to think of cognition in functional and rather practical terms. We remember, reason, judge, imagine, and decide. When these capacities begin to fail in dementia, something deeper may change along with them. People with dementia can certainly retain important aspects of identity and agency even with significant cognitive decline. But Deter’s observation raises a fundamental question.

How much of who we are is connected to the thinking we do?

Artificial intelligence approaches that question from a very different direction. With Alzheimer’s disease, cognition can be involuntarily diminished. With AI, cognition can be expanded while portions of the cognitive work are voluntarily handed somewhere else. The machine becomes a cognitive alternative that remembers, writes, analyzes, and participates in decisions that were once the domain of our human brains.

AI’s output can be extraordinary, yet our own participation in producing that output becomes smaller.

This is the emerging issue of cognitive surrender. The concern isn’t that AI makes us less intelligent or somehow diminishes our humanity. AI can be an extraordinary cognitive partner, and many use it that way every day.

But its growing role in our thinking raises another question about what I would call cognitive selfhood.

AI and cognitive selfhood

Cognitive selfhood is our meaningful participation in the thinking through which we experience and become ourselves. It doesn’t require that every thought originate independently inside our heads—that was never true. Teachers, books, conversations, and culture have always shaped our thinking. But I believe that AI introduces something different in degree and perhaps eventually in kind. It can enter the production of an idea before that idea has fully formed within us. It can complete the argument, suggest the judgment, and sometimes provide the thought itself.

This creates a curious inversion. In dementia, cognitive capacity can decline, and the experience of self can become disrupted along with it. With AI, our cognitive capacity can increase dramatically even as our participation in that cognition decreases. We may know more and reason more effectively while becoming less certain about where our own cognition ends and another intelligence begins.

This is where the idea of a human right becomes relevant, although perhaps in a more fundamental sense than we typically use the term. And to be clear, I’m not arguing for another item in a legal or political catalog of rights. I’m thinking about something that comes before the catalog itself. As AI becomes increasingly capable of participating in our thinking, there may be something fundamental worth preserving.

We must preserve our participation in the cognitive processes that help constitute who we are

Auguste Deter’s words came from the tragedy of a disease that was taking something from her. AI presents almost the opposite circumstance. We are gaining extraordinary cognitive capability, often willingly and enthusiastically. Yet her words offer a strangely relevant and important warning. If cognition is deeply connected to selfhood, the question isn’t simply how much thinking a machine can do for us. It’s how much of our own thinking we need to retain to remain meaningfully ourselves.

After all, every other human right assumes there is a self there to hold it. And that makes cognitive selfhood something more fundamental than another right on the list. It may be the last human right because, without it, the others begin to lose their meaning.

item.title: When Love Sours
item.description:
Relationships

When Love Sours

How rejection and shame can transform affection into resentment and hostility

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Love can sour when another person’s actions become too closely tied to our own sense of worth and security.
  • Rejection can turn affection into resentment when it threatens our self-worth.
  • We can blame others when facing our own choices feels more painful than blaming them.

In an interview with Alvin P. Sanoff for U.S. News & World Report, Elie Wiesel offered a line I now hear repeated often: "The opposite of love is not hate, it’s indifference." Wiesel’s words capture something important; love and hate keep us emotionally attached, while indifference does not. Yet, I have never found the line entirely satisfying. Love and hate do seem like opposites, even if they share something that indifference doesn’t. Love can motivate us to protect and seek another person’s good. Hatred can direct that same attention in the opposite direction—toward punishment or harm.

A better way to think about the relationship may be to borrow from Aristotle’s golden mean. While the mean is often misunderstood as splitting the difference between extremes, Aristotle does not explain it like a mathematical midpoint. Virtue requires responding to the right thing, for the right reasons, and to the right degree. Vice is when some part of that response is off.

Like Aristotle’s account of virtue, our feelings toward another person can vary in intensity and in how they are directed. With love and hate, the other person still matters to us, but that concern points in very different directions. With indifference, the motivating force largely disappears.

How Rejection Turns Affection to Hostility

When we love someone, we develop expectations. We hope they will care for us, prioritize our needs, and see us in ways that matter to us. Problems arise, however, when those hopes become requirements for how the other person must act for us to feel secure. Disappointment can feel like rejection, and rejection can feel like a threat.

A 2010 review of experimental and diary research found that people high in rejection sensitivity are particularly likely to respond to perceived rejection with hostility and reactive aggression. A 2023 meta-analysis of 60 studies similarly linked greater rejection sensitivity with more relationship conflict, jealousy, and intimate-partner violence, as well as less satisfaction and closeness.

This does not mean rejection automatically turns love into hate, but it can change how we relate to someone, especially if we are rejection sensitive. When we repeatedly interpret our partner’s behavior as failing to meet our expectations or rejecting us, we may care what they do, but now our attention is focused on resentment and hostility rather than affection.

Emily Brontë’s Wuthering Heights dramatizes this transformation well. When Catherine chooses Edgar rather than Heathcliff, Heathcliff’s fixation does not disappear. It becomes entangled with revenge. His life remains organized around Catherine, but no longer around seeking her good. His love sours when Catherine can no longer occupy the place he imagined for her in his life.

Do You Hate Them or Who You Became Around Them?

Sometimes resentment is less about what the other person did and more about what their presence forces us to see in ourselves.

We may have acted selfishly, become dependent or subservient in ways that we are ashamed of, or compromised values we cared about. The other person can then become associated with things we would rather forget. Hating them becomes easier than facing ourselves.

Research by June Tangney and colleagues has connected shame-proneness with anger, hostility, and the externalization of blame. More recent research also supports the contention that shame can contribute to aggression through hostility and blaming others.

The move from self-reflection to blaming others comes when our memories, and how we interpret our own experiences, become conveniently self-serving. We remember our own hurt while emphasizing what the other person did wrong. We explain our own failures by pointing to circumstances while treating theirs as evidence of who they are.

The horror film, Together, offers a vivid metaphor for this phenomenon. Tim and Millie become so entwined that they don't know where one ends and the other begins. Each becomes connected to the other’s disappointments and the person they have become. Their literal fusion is a visual metaphor for the psychological lesson that when we cannot separate who we are from who we are with. We regret who we became, which can lead to resentment towards them.

Not Letting Love Sour

Rejection and shame look dissimilar, but they can make us feel differently towards our loved ones; both tempt us to give up responsibility for maintaining our own sense of worth. This does not mean we should love less or stay detached so rejection never hurts. Or that another person can never make us change how we see ourselves. The challenge is learning what we can reasonably ask of others when love makes us vulnerable.

We can feel rejection without turning hurt into hostility. We can confront shame without making another person the villain of a story we helped write. Maybe love’s hardest demand is to recognize that while someone else can enrich our life, they are not responsible for it. Our life is still our own, and their life still belongs to them.

item.title: Let Go of Fixing Your Partner's Defensiveness
item.description:
Relationships

Let Go of Fixing Your Partner's Defensiveness

Everything changes when you stop struggling to make a partner "get it."

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Remember that your partner’s anger and defensiveness are about them—not you.
  • Stop trying to fix or change a defensive partner; instead, accept their limitation as reality.
  • Respond like a “stone”: stay calm, don’t react, and avoid validating their narrative.
Source: SrdjanVrebac / Shutterstock

So far in this series, I’ve been looking at anger and defensiveness in relationships, and specifically the habitual responses we fall into to try and manage and survive it. Now I want to offer some action steps, boots-on-the-ground strategies to change your relationship with your partner’s anger—and with yourself in the face of it.

When anger and defensiveness arise in this other person, remember that they are not actually seeing you in those moments; you are just an inverted mirror for them. They project their self-criticism, loathing, shame, and everything else they don’t want to feel or see about themselves onto you. While it doesn’t make it okay that they behave this way, remember, their rage belongs to and is about them—not you.

Epictetus, the Greek Stoic philosopher, had some helpful advice when it came to dealing with anger, which is as applicable today as it was when he offered it over 2,000 years ago. In short, Epictetus counseled that when you’re being deluged with someone else’s rage, listen like a stone. Don’t defend yourself or try to set the record straight. Don’t attempt to bring rationality into an irrational situation. Behave like a stone. Stones are not bothered by anyone else’s choices; you can shout at them, and they remain unperturbed and unchanged.

Remember, when someone is in a defensive episode, they want you to react, to bite the hook and get pulled into their story. They’re baiting you to start defending yourself, going after them, and joining them in their “code red.” Your emotional reactivity allows them to validate their victimhood: “See what you’re doing to me?”

The root of your suffering, in part, comes from the expectation that a rational request should bring a rational response. This is not to say that it’s not profoundly disappointing, enraging, and saddening that your partner behaves like this, and yet, when someone is emotionally immature and insecure, to believe that they would respond in any way other than immaturely and defensively is… madness. It is to expect a fragile person to act in a non-fragile way.

The work is recognizing this expectation inside yourself, and seeing their ego fragility and inability to hear feedback as disabilities, like any other. In the same way that you would not expect a blind person to be able to drive a car, you cannot expect or make someone who is emotionally immature behave in a sensible and sensitive manner. This person doesn’t have the capacity to tolerate responsibility. It’s not going to happen.

Treat their limitation as a what-is and expect behavior that aligns with that reality. While it’s heartbreaking to accept that you’re not going to get what you want from this person, it’s also liberating to let go of the expectation that a different outcome is possible. When you stop fighting with reality, you might also decide that you want to change your life, which might include your relationship.

It’s important, too, to change your response when they go into victim mode, withdraw, or go silent to punish you for telling them they hurt you. Don’t bite the hook or chase after them; don’t play the character they’ve written for you in their dysfunctional story. Let them do what they need to do; turn your attention to your own life and what you need to do to establish independence and create well-being for yourself. Leave them to play out their drama in their cave of blindness.

If they switch into attack mode and blame you, trying to make you feel guilty for telling them they hurt you, hold your ground. Continue repeating the same sentence that states what happened that’s not okay with you.

When they distort your words or veer off topic, use simple language in response: “That’s not actually what I said,” “We can discuss my shortcomings another time, but right now I want to focus on now.” But always come back to the same script that states what you’re upset about now, what you need, and what you don’t want in the relationship any longer. Keep a flat, robotic tone. Behave like you’re coated in Teflon—an impenetrable stone. Imagine that you’re with a toddler having a tantrum, which, in fact, you are—only it's an adult toddler who may also be your partner.

Do not apologize for what you haven’t done. Instead, hold the ground of your truth and stay connected to your own needs; hold on to yourself right there in the eye of their tsunami.

Finally, know that you don’t ever need permission to exit a conversation that feels damaging or poisonous to you. You can always suggest that you “revisit the issue later,” as you “think you both need some space at the moment.” Remember, you are responsible for your own well-being; you are your own caretaker—choose to be that caretaker for yourself. No one has the right to harm you.

This knowing is so important I’ll say it again—no one has the right to harm you. You always have the right to create a physical boundary, to walk out of the room and create distance from their toxic energy. As Marcus Aurelius, the second-century Roman Emperor and Stoic philosopher, taught, you may share a physical space with this other person, but you don’t have to give them access to your internal mental or emotional space.

A Cheat Sheet for Responding to Anger and Defensiveness

Don’t:

  • Try to figure out how to make the other person change or “get it.”
  • Try to get them to “hear” you or take responsibility for their actions.
  • Take care of them and reassure them that all is well.
  • Defend yourself, attack back, or engage in their distorted storyline.
  • Assume responsibility for their anger.
  • Feel guilty for having needs.
  • Try to “win them back” when they withdraw or stonewall.
  • Wait for them to apologize or feel empathy.
  • Expect an emotionally disabled person to behave with wisdom and awareness.
  • Deny the reality of how you feel and who they are.
  • Indulge the fantasy that it will be different next time and give the broken system one more try.
  • Let them access your mental and emotional space.

DO:

  • Stop trying to make them “hear” you.
  • Start establishing independence—emotionally, physically, socially, and financially.
  • Trust your truth and intuition: if it feels bad for you, it’s bad for you.
  • Remind yourself that you’re allowed to have needs. Needs are healthy.
  • Pause to feel your feelings, instead of rushing to fix the situation.
  • Practice staying quiet and feeling what’s happening inside your body when you would normally rush to fill in the silence.
  • Remind yourself that you’re learning to tolerate discomfort and uncertainty in the face of conflict—to get okay with not being okay.
  • Honor yourself each time you do things differently, when you break an old habit, and refrain from cleaning up the mess the other person created. Acknowledge your own efforts to change a situation that doesn’t work for you.

item.title: Is Boredom Behind “Out of Control” Sexual Behavior?
item.description:
Sex

Is Boredom Behind “Out of Control” Sexual Behavior?

When life doesn't feel stimulating enough, sex can become a coping mechanism.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Boredom occurs when we don’t perceive our environment as being stimulating enough.
  • More than a dozen studies find that hypersexual people report greater feelings of boredom in general.
  • Feeling bored with one's sex life specifically may also predict hypersexuality.
  • The boredom-hypersexuality link may have implications for treatment of "out of control" sexual behavior.
Source: Joel Lee / Unsplash

Over the years, a number of possible causes and triggers of “hypersexual” or “out of control” sexual behavior have been proposed. One of the many factors under consideration is feelings of boredom.

Boredom is a negative psychological mood state that occurs when we don’t perceive our environment as being stimulating enough. Boredom is, of course, subjective because two people can experience the same environment in very different ways. What is stimulating to one person may be boring to another.

Some people may be more easily predisposed to boredom. For example, people high in sensation-seeking tendencies may get bored easily due to their heightened need for novelty and excitement. Also, people feeling depressed or lonely might report feelings of boredom stemming from those negative emotional states.

At the same time, there’s a feedback loop: While sensation-seeking tendencies, depression, and loneliness might lead to feelings of boredom, feeling bored in and of itself could trigger all of these things.

Regardless of the reason, when people feel bored, they often seek out ways of relieving that negative mood state. And turning to sex might be one such coping strategy.

Is There a Scientific Link Between Boredom and Hypersexuality?

In a paper published in The Journal of Sexual Medicine, researchers scoured the literature for existing studies reporting links between boredom and hypersexuality.

“Hypersexuality” is a controversial construct that different people define in different ways, with some characterizing it as “sexual addiction,” sexual compulsivity, or sexual impulsivity. However, a common thread running through all of these definitions is the idea that hypersexuality involves high levels of sexual behavior that one feels are “out of control.”

Researchers identified 19 studies examining the potential link between boredom and hypersexuality. Of them, 15 established an association, while just four did not. Thus, the weight of the evidence suggests that hypersexual people do tend to report more feelings of boredom.

For example, one study (based primarily on heterosexually identified men) found that 71 percent of participants reported that they “use online sexual activities to manage boredom.” Likewise, in a study of men who have sex with men, researchers found that using sex to cope with boredom, stress, and/or concentration issues was the strongest predictor of hypersexual behavior.

In addition, several case studies that involved qualitative interviews found that people often pointed to boredom and having time on their hands as causes of their sexual urges and desires.

One study also found that, in both men and women, being prone to boredom was a predictor of higher levels of masturbation.

It wasn’t just general feelings of boredom that were linked to hypersexuality, though. Feelings of sexual boredom specifically also predicted hypersexuality. This suggests that having a routine and predictable sex life is another aspect of boredom that could prompt more sex-seeking behavior.

What We Still Don’t Know

There are some important limitations of the existing research. One is that most studies focused on male participants only, so our understanding of how this link might vary based on gender is somewhat limited.

Another issue is that all of these studies are correlational, which creates issues when it comes to inferring cause and effect. Is it the case that boredom triggers hypersexual behavior, or does hypersexual behavior potentially lead to feelings of boredom, perhaps through a process of habituation to repeated sexual stimulation?

Longitudinal studies could help distinguish between these explanations.

Of course, there’s also a potential third-variable explanation. Perhaps something else (e.g., sensation-seeking tendencies, mood disorders, emotional regulation problems) underlies both boredom and hypersexuality, and maybe that’s what’s really fueling the association.

Takeaways

While we must await the results of further studies, the weight of the current evidence does seem to indicate a fairly reliable link between boredom and hypersexuality, which suggests the possibility that hypersexuality may often stem, in part, from feelings of boredom.

That possibility could have important implications for clinical treatment of hypersexual behavior, something many have referred to by the controversial term “sex addiction” (which is not a formal diagnostic category in the DSM).

Effectively treating people who are distressed about their “out of control” sexual behaviors requires a thorough understanding of the underlying cause(s). Many current treatment approaches view sex itself as the problem; however, a growing amount of research (including the work on boredom discussed here) points to sexual behavior as the symptom.

Consistent with this idea, many sex researchers and therapists have found that patients presenting with “out of control” sexual behavior often have underlying moral conflicts surrounding sex as well as mood disorders such as depression, anxiety, and bipolar disorder.

If sexual behavior is serving as a way to cope with boredom, depression, anxiety, or other difficulties, focusing exclusively on the behavior may miss an important part of the problem.

Developing better treatments means paying more attention to what is driving the behavior—whether that is boredom, moral conflict, a mood disorder, or something else—rather than assuming sex itself is the problem.

item.title: Dolly Parton Lived Life with Generosity
item.description:
Altruism

Dolly Parton Lived Life with Generosity

Five ways to live like Dolly and celebrate her spirit.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Dolly lived a life of generosity, joy, love, and laughter.
  • We can learn a lot from her altruism and humble spirit.
  • Living like Dolly means supporting people in need and bringing people together.

Dolly Parton’s tragic passing on August 25, 2026, marks the end of an era. She lived with generosity, joy, love, and laughter. Her heart was so big that it is hard to imagine the amazing things she accomplished in her lifetime. How can we live like Dolly and celebrate her spirit? Here are five ways:

Dolly Parton in a 1970 RCA Records press photo
Source: RCA Records/Public Domain

1. Support People in Need.

Dolly was an iconic philanthropist. She founded the Imagination Library that mails free books to children. She established the My People Fund to provide monthly $1,000 checks to families who lost their homes to devastating wildfires in East Tennessee. She opened Dollywood and provided thousands of jobs in Tennessee. Dolly even donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center, helping fund the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine, and later donated yet another $1 million to support research on pediatric infectious diseases.

Living like Dolly means helping others and supporting those in need. And you don’t need millions of dollars to do it. Volunteer at a local food bank, help out at a local library, see what your community needs, and give back.

2. Promote Empathy.

Dolly was an oil well of emotional support, strength, and empathy to those around her. She had a strict policy that “no one ever cries alone” in her presence. She always saw the importance of reaching out to others and building compassionate relationships. For Dolly, everyone deserved a shoulder to cry on.

Living like Dolly means recognizing others' emotions and being there for them when they are down. Reach out to those around you and provide emotional support—a helping hand, a soft smile, and a warm cup of tea is sometimes all someone needs.

3. Find Joy and Beauty Everywhere.

One of Dolly’s songs, “Coat of Many Colors,” describes the joy she had while wearing a jacket made from an old box of rags. While many may have seen this coat as a sign of poverty, Parton sings about how much she loved it. To Dolly, joy and beauty were everywhere—and they were to be celebrated. Living like Dolly means finding joy in the little things and seeing beauty in places where you might not expect it. Slow down and smell the roses, touch grass, and listen.

4. Be Humble.

An undercover Dolly once entered a “Dolly impersonator” Drag Queen Lookalike Contest—and lost! In fact, she didn’t even place in the contest. But Dolly took it in stride and sashayed away, paying it no mind. For Dolly, having a drag queen win this contest was a true homage to her spirit. Living like Dolly means being humble and recognizing the amazing people around you doing incredible things. Take a minute to drink in the spirit of those in your orbit and celebrate them for who they are.

5. Bring People Together.

Dolly was an icon to so many people—country music lovers, feminists, blondes, comedians, queer communities, and so much more. She dominated the entertainment industry through her entrepreneurship and business savvy. Her music and films reached so many people, bridging cultural divides and promoting unity. If one thing sums up Dolly, it is that she brought people together.

Living like Dolly also means recognizing our shared humanity. When we see each other through a collective lens, we can get through the ups and downs and work together. We can build community and a shared sense of connection.
